description: This figure group is composite, pairing a rendered numeric table with a two-series scatter/line plot. The table (Table II, "Typical tensile properties of some conventional sheet steels currently used in automotives") has columns Steel, YS (MPa), UTS (MPa), UE (%), TE (%), n and r̄ (bar-r), and eight rows: IF-Rephos, ULC-BH340, HSLA350, DP500, DP600, DP800, TRIP600 and TRIP780. YS rises from 217 MPa (IF-Rephos) to 505 MPa (TRIP780) and UTS from 345 MPa to 834 MPa (DP800); UE spans 12.3-23.9 % and TE 17.9-41.6 %; n lies between 0.13 and 0.26, and r̄ is given where available (0.83 to 2.1). Fig. 12 plots Young's modulus in GPa (y-axis, 140-220) against Al content in wt.% (x-axis, 0-10). Two literature datasets are marked: blue circles labelled "Rana et al. [6, 20]", whose points fall from about 204 GPa at 0 wt.% Al, through roughly 163 and 158 GPa, to about 153 GPa near 10 wt.%; and red triangles labelled "Frommeyer et al. [18]" at roughly 6-9 wt.% Al, falling from about 191 GPa to about 170 GPa. Both series decrease monotonically with increasing Al. The panels jointly argue that high-Al low-density steels compete with conventional automotive sheet steels on tensile properties, but Al addition lowers Young's modulus and hence stiffness.

subfigures.description: A scatter/line plot of Young's modulus (GPa, y-axis 140-220) versus Al content (wt.%, x-axis 0-10). Blue circles (Rana et al. [6, 20]) decrease from about 204 GPa at 0 wt.% Al to about 153 GPa near 10 wt.%. Red triangles (Frommeyer et al. [18]) occupy 6-9 wt.% Al and fall from about 191 GPa to about 170 GPa. Both trends show a monotonic reduction of Young's modulus with Al addition; no numeric data labels are printed at the points.

observations.observation: The table's data body consists of eight conventional automotive sheet steels: IF-Rephos, ULC-BH340, HSLA350, DP500, DP600, DP800, TRIP600 and TRIP780.
Table column headers are Steel, YS (MPa), UTS (MPa), UE (%), TE (%), n and r̄ (bar-r).
Within the table, UTS increases from 345 MPa for IF-Rephos to 834 MPa for DP800, while total elongation TE decreases from 41.6 % to 17.9 % over the same ranking.
Table values DP800 shows the highest UTS (834 MPa) with the lowest UE (12.3 %) and TE (17.9 %), whereas IF-Rephos shows the lowest YS/UTS (217/345 MPa) with the highest TE (41.6 %).
The r̄ (Lankford) column is populated only for some steels (2.1 for ULC-BH340, 1.1 for HSLA350, 0.83 DP500, 0.86 DP600, 0.93 TRIP600) and shown as a dash for IF-Rephos, DP800 and TRIP780.
Fig. 12 plots Young's modulus (GPa) on the y-axis spanning 140 to 220 against Al content (wt.%) on the x-axis spanning 0 to 10.
Fig. 12 contains two labelled datasets: blue circles 'Rana et al. [6, 20]' and red triangles 'Frommeyer et al. [18]'.
In Fig. 12 both datasets trend monotonically downward with increasing Al content, with the blue circle series spanning roughly 204 GPa at 0 wt.% Al to about 153 GPa near 10 wt.% Al.
The caption states Fig. 12 shows the reduction of Young's modulus in low-density steels as a result of Al addition, citing refs 6, 18 and 20.

The caption describes the table as typical tensile properties of conventional sheet steels used in automotives, noting the steels are identified by commercial names whose abbreviations are defined in the article text and whose trailing numbers denote tensile strength levels.

The citing text asserts that Al addition causes the Young's modulus of steels to decrease, which can negatively influence the use of low-density steels in automotives because Young's modulus directly controls stiffness.
The citing text asserts that high-Al-containing steels are comparable with, or better than, conventional automotive steels in terms of mechanical properties.

unreadable_items: Fig. 12 data points carry no printed numeric labels; their values can only be positioned relative to the y-axis gridlines (140-220 GPa) and are therefore approximate readings, not printed numbers.
